title: A Locally Tokenized Generative Model for Robust Time-Series Watermarking
claim: Different post-edit attacks shift a detector's null statistic in opposite directions, so a fixed clean-calibrated threshold gives unreliable false positives.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right: stacked token strips, then overlaid histograms with threshold line
description: Panel (a) has two stacked strip plots. Each shows features on the y-axis and timesteps 0–128 on the x-axis. The cells are red or green, marking recovered red/green token assignments. The top strip is non-watermarked data after a 30% crop, with 40.6% green and 59.4% red, so it is mostly red. The bottom strip is the same data after a 30% insert, with 59.9% green and 40.1% red, so it is mostly green. Panel (b) is an overlaid histogram of z-scores, with count on the y-axis. A gray distribution of unattacked non-watermarked samples is centered near 0. A red crop distribution sits far to the left, around -4. A blue insert distribution sits to the right, around 3.8. A dashed red vertical threshold line falls inside the blue distribution, and a legend reports TPR and mean for each. The eye goes first to the opposing red and blue histograms around the threshold.
caption: Bidirectional drift of the null on non-watermarked samples (TimeWak [ref], Stocks). Crop and insert push the recovered tokens (a) and the resulting $z$-score (b) in opposite directions, with insert crossing the clean-calibrated threshold and yielding an $85%$ false-positive rate.
abstract: Watermarking is a central tool for provenance in generative models, yet its application to multivariate time series remains hindered by reliability failures under post-editing attacks. We show that existing detectors, which rely on globally coupled re-encoding, suffer from bidirectional drift of the null distribution: post-editing attacks can shift the $z$-score of non-watermarked samples in either direction, invalidating clean-calibrated thresholds. We argue that this instability is a property of the re-encoding, and that reliable detection requires each recovered unit to depend only on a bounded temporal neighborhood. Guided by this principle, we propose L-VQVAE, a generative model in which each discrete token is produced from a short contiguous window, and LVQMark, a watermarking method over this token space that combines logit-bias injection with robust re-encoding for attack-time detection. Experiments on four benchmarks spanning finance, energy, and neuroimaging show that our approach preserves generation quality while stabilizing both detection power and false-positive behavior under post-editing attacks.
